nameStory: The Beaugregory gets its charming name from "beau," meaning handsome in French, combined with "gregory" - a reference to the scientific genus name Stegastes and possibly honoring early naturalists. This little fish earned the "handsome" part of its name thanks to its bright, eye-catching colors that make it stand out like a jewel on the seafloor.
description: The Beaugregory is a small, colorful damselfish that's a rare tropical visitor to New England waters. These compact fish typically grow to about 4 inches long and sport a deep, oval-shaped body that's built for darting between rocks and coral. With their bright yellow bodies often marked with blue spots or stripes, they're unmistakable when you do spot one. In New England, they're almost always juveniles that have traveled north with warm currents during summer months.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow body with electric blue markings, especially around the head and fins - the colors are so vivid they almost seem to glow underwater

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, compressed oval body that feels solid and muscular when handled, like a small yellow pancake with attitude

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish, typically 2-4 inches long in New England waters - about the size of a large goldfish cracker

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Large, fan-like dorsal and anal fins with sharp spines that can prick your finger if you're not careful handling them

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found near rocky bottoms, jetties, or artificial reefs in shallow coastal waters where they can quickly duck into crevices

habitat: In New England, Beaugregorys are extremely rare visitors found only in shallow coastal waters with rocky or structured bottoms, particularly around jetties, breakwaters, and nearshore reefs. They prefer areas with plenty of hiding spots and are most likely to be encountered in southern New England waters during the warmest months. These tropical fish require warm water temperatures and are typically only found when strong currents carry them northward from their usual Caribbean range.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare; any sightings would be exceptional and likely represent fish that somehow survived the winter in unusually warm pockets.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for potential sightings as warm Gulf Stream currents may carry juveniles northward to New England waters during the hottest months.
seasonality.fall: Possible but declining as water temperatures begin to drop; any fish present will not survive the coming winter.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters due to cold temperatures that are lethal to this tropical species.

funFact: Beaugregorys are feisty little farmers that cultivate their own algae gardens by removing unwanted plants and aggressively chasing away other fish - including species many times their size - from their underwater plots!
confusionNotes: In New England waters, the bright yellow coloration makes Beaugregorys nearly impossible to confuse with native species, though they might be mistaken for escaped tropical aquarium fish. Remember: if you see a brilliant yellow fish with blue markings in New England waters, you're likely looking at something very special and very far from home.
contextualKnowledge: The incredibly low observation count of just 2 in New England reflects how truly unusual these sightings are - Beaugregorys are warm-water fish that are only occasionally carried north by ocean currents, making any New England encounter a noteworthy event worth reporting to local marine biologists.
compareHints: The Beaugregory can be distinguished from its close relative the Bicolor Damselfish by its uniform bright yellow coloration, while the Bicolor Damselfish has a distinct two-toned appearance with a dark front half and bright yellow rear. Both are extremely rare in New England, but Beaugregorys maintain their golden color throughout their bodies rather than showing the sharp color division of their bicolor cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The bicolor damselfish differs from its relative the beaugregory by its distinct two-tone coloration pattern, while beaugregorys show more uniform coloring with blue and yellow highlights.
